title: Survival up. Did anyone live longer?
hook: A new test makes more people alive 5 years after diagnosis. Does that mean longer lives?

doesNotKnow: that the survival clock starts at diagnosis, so finding an illness earlier raises this count even when nobody lives a day longer (lead time)

misconception: If more people are alive 5 years after diagnosis, they must be living longer.
objective: The learner can explain that in a group of 14 whose deaths do not move, finding the illness 3 years earlier raises 'alive 5 years after diagnosis' from 6 to 12 because only the start of the clock moved (lead time), and that comparing deaths in whole groups is not fooled by this.

claims.text: In the model, with no test 6 of 14 (43%) are alive 5 years after diagnosis; with the test finding the illness 3 years earlier, 12 of 14 (86%), with every death on the same day.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Node, own copy: T = 1.25 ... 7.75 (14 values); count of T + L > 5: L 0 -> 6 (43%), 0.5 -> 7, 1 -> 8, 1.5 -> 9, 2 -> 10, 2.5 -> 11, 3 -> 12 (86%). Options 43% / 64% / 86% match 6/14, 9/14, 12/14. Death positions X(t) do not depend on L in the code.

claims.text: Finding an illness earlier raises survival counted from diagnosis even when nobody lives longer; this is called lead time. Only the start of the clock moves.
claims.source: Definition of lead time: survival is measured from diagnosis, so moving diagnosis earlier while death is fixed lengthens measured survival by construction.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: survival counted from diagnosis is (death - diagnosis); moving diagnosis earlier by L with death fixed adds L to every survival time, so 'alive 5 years after diagnosis' can only rise. Shown by c1 with all crosses fixed.

claims.text: To judge an earlier test, compare deaths in whole groups.
claims.source: In the model, death dates do not depend on the test, so deaths per group are unaffected by when diagnosis happens. Optional context, not on the card: Welch, Schwartz and Woloshin 2000, JAMA 283(22). Unverified: needs a human source check including the citation.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation, general not just in the toy: a whole group's death count or death rate over a fixed period never refers to the diagnosis date, so moving diagnosis earlier cannot change it; it is immune to lead time by construction. The cited Welch, Schwartz and Woloshin 2000 was not opened and the verdict does not rest on it. Non-blocking: the recall's 'fair way' (compare whole scanned and unscanned groups) is fair only if the groups are alike, as in a randomised trial; 'randomly assigned groups' would be more exact (cm-life's call).

claims.text: 14 people with a made-up illness, found when symptoms start, each dying 1 to 8 years later; treatment changes nothing. This toy makes no claim about any real test.
claims.source: Invented model (brief), stated on the stage, in the question and in the reveal. No advice about screening.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention, stated on the locked stage ('14 people with a made-up illness ... dies 1 to 8 years later'), in the question ('Treatment changes nothing') and the reveal ('This toy makes no claim about any real test'). T runs 1.25 to 7.75, inside '1 to 8 years'.

claims.text: Recall keyed option 'Compare death rates in randomly assigned scanned and unscanned groups'; why: 'Survival counted from diagnosis rises whenever diagnosis moves earlier, even if no death moves; deaths in randomly assigned groups do not depend on when diagnosis happened.'
claims.source: Lead time (c2) and c3: a group's death count over a fixed period never refers to the diagnosis date. Random assignment makes the scanned and unscanned groups alike apart from the scan, so a difference in deaths is the scan's effect (fact-checker pass 38, c3 note).
claims.note: Reset to unverified by demo-builder (2026-10-15): W-867 optional wording: recall keyed option and why now say 'randomly assigned groups' (was 'whole groups'), so the comparison is fair only when the groups are alike. New claim: the recall was not recorded before. | FC pass 42 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): DISPUTED. The keyed option ('Compare death rates in randomly assigned scanned and unscanned groups') is right and follows from c2/c3, and both distractors are wrong. The why's second clause, 'deaths in randomly assigned groups do not depend on when diagnosis happened', is false as written. If finding the disease 2 years sooner lets treatment work, deaths in the scanned group do depend on the earlier diagnosis, and that dependence is exactly what the trial is meant to detect. Read literally, the clause says the trial could never show a benefit. What is true (and what the claim's own source says) is that a group's death count over a fixed period is not counted from the diagnosis date, so lead time alone cannot inflate it. Minor: 'rises whenever diagnosis moves earlier' overstates it. Survival from diagnosis can only stay level or rise when diagnosis moves earlier, and it rises when someone crosses the 5-year line; in this card it 'jumps'. Fix (demo-builder; lesson owner's wording): 'Survival counted from diagnosis rises when diagnosis moves earlier, even if no death moves. Death rates in randomly assigned groups are not counted from diagnosis, so only a real change in deaths moves them.' Then this verifies.

recall.question: A clinic starts a scan that finds a disease 2 years sooner. Its 5-year survival jumps. What is the fair way to tell whether the scan helps?
options: Compare death rates in randomly assigned scanned and unscanned groups
Count how many more cases the scan finds
recall.why: Survival counted from diagnosis rises whenever diagnosis moves earlier, even if no death moves; deaths in randomly assigned groups do not depend on when diagnosis happened.
